lessons.point: Scanning an MCP config can run code, because the scanner starts each stdio (standard input/output) server with the command in the config. Scan untrusted configs only inside a sandbox.
lessons.excerpt: Agent Scan starts stdio MCP servers by executing the commands in the config and connects to configured remote MCP server URLs with their configured headers.

lessons.point: The scanner blocks link-local and cloud-metadata addresses for remote MCP calls, but it admits that DNS rebinding is still possible.
lessons.excerpt: DNS is validated before each request, but resolution again at connection time leaves a DNS-rebinding window.

lessons.point: Fleet (background) mode inspects remote servers without asking. By default, though, it does not start local stdio (standard input/output) servers.
lessons.excerpt: Background and push-key scans continue to inspect remote servers automatically for fleet coverage, but do not start stdio servers unless

lessons.point: Analysis runs in the cloud. Tool descriptions, MCP configs and skill content leave the machine, with secrets redacted first.
lessons.excerpt: It sends the component information needed for analysis, including agent application details, MCP server configurations and signatures, tool names and descriptions, and skill content.

entries.takeaway: Agent Scan gives a quick inventory of agent supply-chain risk on a machine, but the scan itself can run code and send data out, so plan for that.

actionable.title: Run Snyk Agent Scan in a disposable sandbox
actionable.detail: Run `uvx snyk-agent-scan@latest` (needs SNYK_TOKEN) inside a container or VM when you scan untrusted MCP configs. Review each consent prompt, and never pass --dangerously-run-mcp-servers outside a sandbox. Use --ci for a non-zero exit code. Do not parse specific risk names, because the output schema is experimental. Check with your data policy before use, since skill content and tool descriptions go to Snyk's API.

entries.verify_note: Lessons supported by the README; redaction covers secret values only, and the toxic-flows wording is from the v0.5 capability list.
entries.prior_art: Invariant Labs mcp-scan (the tool's predecessor) and the existing archive entry for this repo; Cisco AI Defense mcp-scanner
entries.threat: Malicious or poisoned MCP servers and agent skills: prompt injection in tool descriptions, hidden malware payloads, credential leaks.
entries.conditions: Developers install third-party MCP servers and skills into coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot.
entries.mitigations: Scan the agent components installed on each machine. Run the scanner in a sandbox when configs are untrusted, approve each server before it is contacted, and use fleet background scanning for central monitoring.
entries.author: snyk

entries.title: AegisGate is a self-hosted proxy that filters LLM API traffic
entries.summary: AegisGate is an open-source gateway that sits between agents or apps and upstream LLM APIs. It filters requests and responses with regex-based prompt injection detection, secret and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, tool-call and privilege guards, and output sanitization. Semantic review is optional and runs only on gray-zone cases. By default, its conversation routes run only 13 of its 59 redaction patterns, and a passthrough token mode turns every filter off.

lessons.point: The redaction defaults are narrower than the '50+ patterns' headline. Conversation routes run a credential-only subset unless you opt in to the full set.
lessons.excerpt: by default only the credential-only `redaction.relaxed_pii_ids` subset runs there (13 of the 59 shipped patterns

lessons.point: The core injection detection is mostly pattern matching, with an optional semantic stage. Treat it as one layer of containment, not prevention.
lessons.excerpt: bilingual regex patterns for known injection techniques (direct injection, system prompt exfiltration, typoglycemia obfuscation)

lessons.point: Gateway route suffixes can switch off all filtering. Check that the passthrough mode and numeric port tokens stay internal-only.
lessons.excerpt: `token__passthrough` is treated as internal-only because it disables all filters

lessons.point: Readiness can report healthy while enforcement is degraded, for example with stale rules or an unreachable risk threshold. Monitor the degraded-checks list, not just the HTTP status.
lessons.excerpt: Alert on `degraded_checks` rather than on the status code alone.

entries.takeaway: A useful reference design for an LLM egress proxy, but its default detection is regex and its default redaction is narrow.

actionable.title: Evaluate AegisGate as an egress filter for coding-agent LLM traffic
actionable.detail: Point the agent's base URL at the gateway. Set redaction.relaxed_pii_ids to ["*"] if you need full redaction coverage. Keep AEGIS_ALLOW_PUBLIC_PASSTHROUGH_MODE and AEGIS_ALLOW_PUBLIC_NUMERIC_TOKENS off. Expose admin endpoints only on localhost. Alert on degraded_checks. Treat injection blocking as best effort and keep sandboxing and tool-permission controls in place.

entries.prior_art: Existing entries already cover self-hosted LLM gateways for agents and credential-injecting proxy gateways. LLM Guard and Rebuff are comparable tools.
entries.author: ax128

entries.title: About 80 WhatsApp help pages exposed hidden instructions for Meta's support chatbot
entries.summary: Privacy company Redact found about 80 WhatsApp help and FAQ pages carrying instructions written for Meta's support LLM in their underlying code. The blocks included rules such as not citing privacy laws like GDPR and not suggesting users contact a data protection regulator. Meta blamed a bug and removed the text after WIRED asked; it is unclear how long it was exposed or whether other chatbots could read it.

lessons.point: Instructions written for Meta's chatbot sat in the code of public help pages, so anyone viewing the page source could read them.
lessons.excerpt: exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own.

lessons.point: The leaked rules showed policy steering, such as avoiding privacy regulations even when users raise them.
lessons.excerpt: Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,

lessons.point: The exposure window and whether third-party crawlers or chatbots ingested the text are unknown.
lessons.excerpt: It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed.

lessons.point: The leaked blocks appeared under a recognizable code-block heading.
lessons.excerpt: The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading:

entries.takeaway: Assume any chatbot instructions stored next to public content will eventually be read by the public, so keep them in a separate store and write them as if they will be disclosed.

actionable.title: Keep LLM instructions out of public page payloads
actionable.detail: Serve chatbot instructions and grounding notes from a server-side store, not from hidden blocks in public CMS pages. Add a pre-publish or CI check that scans rendered HTML for known instruction markers (for example a dedicated include tag) and fails the build if it finds one. Review instructions on the assumption they will become public.

entries.prior_art: System-prompt extraction and leak collections (for example published leaks of the Bing/Sydney and Claude system prompts); this case is accidental exposure through CMS page code, not extraction from the model. Verifier: Many earlier system-prompt leaks and extractions (archive: 'System-prompt extraction remains broadly effective', 'Quoting Claude Opus 5 system prompt'). The new part is passive exposure through public CMS page source, not extraction.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Internal chatbot instructions published in public web page code by a CMS bug.
entries.conditions: LLM grounding or instruction blocks stored inside the same CMS content that renders public help pages.
entries.mitigations: Store instructions separately from public content; scan rendered pages for instruction markers before publishing; write instructions assuming disclosure.

entries.title: Cisco AI Defense mcp-scanner checks MCP servers with YARA, LLM and API engines
entries.summary: Cisco's open-source mcp-scanner checks the tools, prompts, resources and server instructions of an MCP server. It uses three engines, which can run together or alone: YARA (a pattern-matching rule language), an LLM-based analyzer and the Cisco AI Defense API. It also scans server source code for suspicious behavior, checks dependencies with pip-audit, looks up bundled files on VirusTotal, and handles MCP 2.0 protocol negotiation. A static mode scans pre-exported JSON files, so it can run in CI without connecting to a live server.

lessons.point: Pattern rules alone miss things, so the scanner pairs YARA (a pattern-matching rule language) with LLM judgment to catch malicious tool descriptions.
lessons.excerpt: The MCP Scanner combines Cisco AI Defense inspect API, YARA rules and LLM-based analysis to detect malicious MCP tools.

lessons.point: Offline scanning of exported tool definitions lets you gate MCP servers in CI without starting them.
lessons.excerpt: Scan pre-generated JSON files without live server connections - perfect for CI/CD pipelines and air-gapped environments

lessons.point: The protocol probe is read-only. A clean result does not show whether unauthenticated callers can invoke tools.
lessons.excerpt: safe legacy checks for older endpoints. It does not call tools or prove

lessons.point: PyPI package scans analyze code without running it, which avoids install-time payloads.
lessons.excerpt: package code is never executed in either mode.

entries.takeaway: Use mcp-scanner as a gate when admitting MCP servers, but remember that scan-time checks do not prove anything about runtime authorization.

actionable.title: Gate MCP servers in CI with mcp-scanner static mode
actionable.detail: Install it with `uv tool install --python 3.13 cisco-ai-mcp-scanner`. Export the tool, prompt and resource definitions as JSON, then run the `static` subcommand with `--analyzers yara` in CI. Add the LLM analyzer and the `supplychain` and `vulnerable-package` subcommands for servers whose source you can see. Run `--scan-known-configs` on developer machines.

entries.verify_note: Claims match the README after narrowing the never-executes point to PyPI scans; mature tool already in the archive.
entries.prior_art: Existing archive entry for this repo; Invariant/Snyk mcp-scan; NVIDIA SkillSpector YARA rules
entries.threat: Malicious MCP tools, prompts, resources or server instructions, plus vulnerable or malware-laden dependencies bundled with MCP servers.
entries.conditions: Organizations adopt third-party MCP servers without reviewing their descriptions, source or dependencies.
entries.mitigations: Run multi-engine scanning across all MCP surfaces when admitting a server, use offline static scans in CI, run dependency and VirusTotal checks, and test authorization separately from scanning.
entries.author: cisco-ai-defense

entries.kind_reason: Open-source training project rather than an incident; unsure, so story.
entries.title: c-goosen releases PwnGPT, an open-source 16-level prompt injection CTF
entries.summary: PwnGPT is an open-source capture-the-flag (CTF) game where players attack LLM agents across 16 levels to extract each level's password. Levels cover input and output guards, hardened system prompts, multi-modal uploads, SQL through function calling, poisoned plugin descriptions, planted memories and code review injection. It runs on Google ADK agents with RAG, with qwen3 on Ollama by default, and has been run at three events.
entries.takeaway: A ready-made range for teaching prompt injection and testing guardrails, but its defaults are not safe to expose to players.

lessons.point: The CTF ladders prompt-injection skills from simple guards to combined defenses, a useful curriculum for training red-teamers and developers.
lessons.excerpt: An open source prompt injection CTF. Players attack LLM agents across 16 levels

lessons.point: Levels reproduce several agent attack surfaces beyond chat: tool descriptions, memory, code review and web pages.
lessons.excerpt: poisoned plugin descriptions, planted memories, code review injection, and finally every protection combined

lessons.point: The defenses practiced include input and output guards and hardened prompts, plus guard models, so players see which layers fail.
lessons.excerpt: input and output guards, a hardened system prompt, multi-modal uploads (image, audio, PDF and JSON), SQL through function calling, Prompt-Guard models, code execution, web page injection

lessons.point: It can run fully local, with a default local model through Ollama, which keeps cost and data exposure low for workshops.
lessons.excerpt: It runs on Google ADK agents with RAG, using qwen3 on Ollama by default, or Gemini or OpenAI.

actionable.title: Use PwnGPT as a prompt-injection training range
actionable.detail: Clone c-goosen/ai-prompt-ctf and run make run (Docker Engine 25+ and Compose v2.20+ needed) for an internal workshop. Read the hosting-an-event notes first, since the README says the default setup is not safe to expose to players, and add your own levels for your agent stack.

entries.prior_art: data/ai-security.json already has LLMVault, a CTF-style OWASP LLM Top 10 range with Ollama live mode; Gandalf-style prompt-injection games are a long-standing genre.
entries.author: c-goosen

entries.title: Agent Plugins spec adds a 1.1.0 working draft to its packaging standard
entries.summary: Agent Plugins is a vendor-neutral standard for packaging Agent Skills and MCP servers into one distributable plugin, built around a plugin.json manifest plus skill directories. Version 1.0.0 is the published release and 1.1.0 is now a working draft. The README leaves how a client exposes a loaded skill to users or models out of scope.
entries.takeaway: A plugin bundles skill prompts and MCP server configs into one artifact, so review and pin it as one supply-chain unit; this README update adds no new security content.

lessons.point: One plugin package can carry both Agent Skills and MCP servers, so a single compromised package can ship both kinds of component.
lessons.excerpt: It defines a portable package format for Agent Skills and MCP servers.

lessons.point: The spec does not define how a client presents a skill to users or models, so trust and consent decisions are left to each client.
lessons.excerpt: How the client exposes the skill to users or models is outside the Agent Plugins specification.

lessons.point: The only visible change since the earlier entry is a new 1.1.0 working draft next to the 1.0.0 release.
lessons.excerpt: Agent Plugins Specification 1.0.0 is the current published release. Agent Plugins Specification 1.1.0 is a working draft.

actionable.title: Review Agent Plugins as one supply-chain unit
actionable.detail: When adopting plugins in this format, scan the bundled SKILL.md files and the MCP server configs together before install, and pin plugin versions. Read the 1.1.0 draft's diff from 1.0.0 for any new fields that affect signing or permissions.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: the README cannot show that the 1.1.0 draft is the only change since the 2026-08-10 entry, and lesson 2's trust-and-consent reading goes beyond the source.
entries.prior_art: Earlier archive entry on the same repo (agentplugins/agent-plugins-spec, 2026-08-10) describing the 1.0.0 spec
entries.threat: A malicious or compromised plugin delivers both skill instructions and MCP server configs to an agent in one install.
entries.mitigations: Scan skills and MCP configs together, pin plugin versions, and require review before a client loads a new plugin.
entries.author: agentplugins

entries.title: OpenGuardrails proposes one vendor-neutral wire protocol for agent guardrails
entries.author: openguardrails
entries.summary: OpenGuardrails (OGR) is an Apache-2.0 specification that defines how an agent harness or LLM gateway sends each model request and response to a guardrail runtime and gets back a verdict, so detection vendors can compete behind one interface. It models agent traffic in layers, from one model call up to sessions, and also runs a detector benchmark. Integrations fail open by default: if the runtime is unreachable, the agent keeps running.
entries.takeaway: A common guardrail interface could cut integration work, but its fail-open default means an attacker who can block the runtime turns the guardrail off.

lessons.point: The project defines the interface and referees a benchmark; it does not build detection itself.
lessons.excerpt: OGR is **not a guardrail product**: it defines the wire and referees the

lessons.point: Verdicts arrive at the two points where blocking is still possible: before the model sees a request and before the agent acts on a response.
lessons.excerpt: the request before the model sees it, the response before the agent

lessons.point: The default on runtime failure is to proceed, so availability of the guardrail becomes a security property.
lessons.excerpt:
Fail-open by
default: if the runtime is unreachable, your agent keeps running.

actionable.title: If you adopt a remote guardrail, decide fail-open vs fail-closed per tool
actionable.detail: For tools with side effects (writes, payments, shell), configure the integration to fail closed when the guardrail runtime is unreachable, and alert on runtime outages; keep fail-open only for read-only steps.

entries.prior_art: Guardrail interfaces in NeMo Guardrails and LLM gateways (LiteLLM, Higress), and the earlier agentplugins spec; OGR's delta is a vendor-neutral event/verdict wire format with a layered traffic model.
entries.threat: Inconsistent or bypassable guardrail enforcement across agents.
entries.conditions: Organizations running several agents and guardrail vendors.
entries.mitigations: Use a single enforcement point per agent loop and choose fail-closed for side-effecting tools.

entries.title: Red teams found Claude refuses direct election-abuse requests but misses split subtasks
entries.summary: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) and the McCain Institute pressure-tested Claude's election safeguards in the US, Israel and Brazil; Claude reliably refused direct harmful requests. It could miss a deceptive campaign that was broken into audience research, site building, content drafting and distribution planning. Anthropic added classifiers for multi-step misuse and banned accounts in cases including a foreign-run fake news site that pushed Russian, Iranian and North Korean narratives. The post also reports that politics makes up 5.75% of US Claude.ai conversations and policy-violating election requests about 0.002%.
entries.takeaway: Refusing one request at a time does not stop decomposed abuse campaigns, so detection has to correlate activity across requests and accounts.

lessons.point: Splitting a task into harmless-looking pieces gets past per-request refusal even when the direct request is refused.
lessons.excerpt: They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.

lessons.point: Influence operators are using LLMs for content production at the early stages of an operation, where a provider can see it and act.
lessons.excerpt: In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives.

lessons.point: An outside evaluator, the Foundation for American Innovation, found Claude Sonnet 4.5 hedged unevenly and softened right-leaning arguments more often.
lessons.excerpt: the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.

actionable.title: Test guardrails against decomposed campaigns, not only direct requests
actionable.detail: In red-team exercises, break a prohibited objective into subtasks that look benign one at a time (research, site building, drafting, distribution). Run them across sessions and accounts, then check whether the abuse detection connects them. Add classifiers that work across conversations or at account level rather than relying on single-turn refusal.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all facts supported; flagged lesson 3's 'internal score missed it' inference (rewritten). Verifier novelty 40, relevance 55; kept 25.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entry is 'Skill cascading attacks', where a harmful goal split across benign-looking agent skills evades per-skill scanners. This item confirms the same decomposition weakness in a deployed consumer model, found by outside red teams in the election-abuse domain. The rest is product policy and transparency news.
entries.threat: Election abuse such as fake news sites, fake social profiles and financially motivated fabricated news, split into individually harmless requests that per-request refusal does not catch.
entries.conditions: An attacker spreads a deceptive campaign across many separate requests, each of which looks legitimate on its own.
entries.mitigations: Use classifiers that detect novel and multi-step misuse across requests, backed by threat-intelligence review and account bans.

entries.title: Brave Search API lets AI agents pay per query through x402
entries.summary: Brave's Search API now takes x402 payments. A request with no payment gets an HTTP 402 response with the price, and the agent signs a USDC payment on Base and sends the request again, so no account or API key is needed. Each query costs $0.005, Brave runs its own facilitator, and it points users to Stripe's Purl CLI wallet.

lessons.point: With x402, the API key is replaced by a wallet that pays for each request, so an agent's wallet becomes a spending credential. Brave's post describes no spend cap or approval step.
lessons.excerpt: Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication.

lessons.point: The flow is that the server sends a 402 with the price, the agent signs a payment for that amount, and then retries. An agent that signs whatever amount a 402 asks for could be overcharged by a hostile or spoofed endpoint, so put spend limits outside the model.
lessons.excerpt: A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it.

lessons.point: Payment replaces sign-up: no Brave account or plan is needed to use the service.
lessons.excerpt: Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service.

entries.takeaway: Agent wallets that pay per call are now a real, high-traffic integration path, so treat the wallet as a credential with hard spend limits.

actionable.title: Put spend policy outside the model for x402-paying agents
actionable.detail: Before an agent gets a wallet that pays x402 endpoints, enforce limits in the wallet or a proxy, not in the prompt. Set a cap per request, a daily budget, and an allowlist of payee addresses and facilitator domains. Log every signed payment with its receipt, and refuse any 402 whose price is above the published rate.

entries.prior_art: The x402 protocol launch (Coinbase) and the V12 x402 security audit (25 flaws) already in the pool. This item is a vendor adopting x402.
entries.threat: An agent holding a funded wallet can be pushed by injected content or a hostile endpoint into paying arbitrary 402 demands, which drains the wallet.
entries.conditions: The agent signs x402 payments on its own, without a payee allowlist or price ceiling enforced outside the model.
entries.mitigations: Limit the wallet's balance and per-request amounts, allowlist payee addresses and facilitators, compare quoted prices with published rates, and require human approval above a set threshold.
entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed the facts but found an unsupported inference (no per-customer identity or quota); that lesson was rewritten to what the post states. Novelty taken as the verifier's 20.
entries.author: sjdh76

entries.title: Microsoft's November 2026 security update adds task-scoped agent permissions and containers
entries.summary: Microsoft's monthly roundup announces Dynamic Permissions. It gives an AI agent its own authority, limited to its current task and only for as long as the task lasts. Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) is now generally available. It adds an operating-system-enforced least-privilege boundary for local agents on Windows. Defender can now also find more than 50 kinds of local AI agents, and the MCP servers they are configured with, on Windows and macOS.

lessons.point: Agent authority should be tied to the current task and expire when the task ends, not be granted as standing access.
lessons.excerpt: Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires.

lessons.point: Operating-system enforcement is presented as the alternative to trusting the agent to stay inside its boundaries.
lessons.excerpt: Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions

lessons.point: An inventory of local agents and their MCP configurations is becoming a standard feature of endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools.
lessons.excerpt: Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity

entries.takeaway: Large vendors now ship task-scoped permissions and OS-level containment for agents, but this post is a product roundup with no data on how well they work.

actionable.title: Inventory local agents and their MCP configs on endpoints
actionable.detail: If you run Defender, turn on local AI agent discovery and list which agents and configured MCP servers exist on each device. On Windows, pilot MXC policies in validate mode before you enforce them on agent processes. Whatever the vendor, scope agent credentials to a single task with a short lifetime.

entries.verify_note: Mostly repeats Microsoft's October insiders post; only MXC general availability is new. The EDR-trend lesson is an extrapolation, so its confidence is low.
entries.prior_art: Microsoft's 2026-10-19 'agents are your newest insiders' post (Dynamic Permissions, local agent discovery) already in the tracker
entries.threat: AI agents with broad standing access to data, tools, files and network can act outside their task.
entries.conditions: Agents run locally or in the enterprise with permissions wider than their current task needs.
entries.mitigations: Use task-scoped, time-limited agent permissions, OS-enforced containment of agent processes, risk-adaptive conditional access with human approval for high-impact actions, and an endpoint inventory of agents and their MCP servers.

entries.kind_reason: Reference architecture and governance guidance, not a single-product bug or patch.
entries.title: Microsoft's AI Citadel blueprint layers gateway, identity and Defender controls for agents
entries.summary: Microsoft's Azure Samples repo describes a four-layer reference architecture for governing AI agents: an API gateway enforcing policy on every model and tool call, agent operations with traces and guardrails, an agent registry with identity, and a Defender, Purview, and Entra security foundation. It argues that agents need their own identities and that the same guardrail should be enforceable at more than one layer. The text is largely Microsoft product framing with little technical depth.

lessons.point: Traditional network and endpoint controls cannot see agent intent, so agent systems need controls that understand prompts and actions, not just packets.
lessons.excerpt: Traditional security inspects packets, headers, and endpoints

lessons.point: Agents should get their own policy-aware identities rather than reusing shared service accounts, so calls can be attributed to a specific agent.
lessons.excerpt: Agents are not users and they are not applications.

lessons.point: Overlapping enforcement points (gateway, runtime, monitoring) mean traffic that bypasses one control is still covered by another.
lessons.excerpt: Same risk, multiple enforcement points — if one control can't apply or is bypassed, another does.

lessons.point: A central gateway can lose the identity of the calling agent, so attribution needs a separate registry or identity layer.
lessons.excerpt: Most AI calls reach models via proxies or gateways

entries.takeaway: A vendor reference for layering gateway policy, agent identity, and monitoring; useful as a checklist, with no new attack or defense.

actionable.title: Check that agent traffic is attributable and enforced in two places
actionable.detail: For your agent stack, verify each model and tool call is logged with an agent identity (not a shared key). Then confirm at least two independent enforcement points (for example gateway content filtering plus runtime guardrails) so a bypass of one does not remove coverage.

entries.prior_art: data/ai-security.json line ~11429: 'Microsoft launches Perception and agent-governance tools at Ignite, framing agents as insiders'; also 'Harden LiteLLM and similar AI gateways' and 'Pin and audit AI gateway installs'. This README mostly restates the same governance framing in a layered form.

entries.title: MCP specification repository now points to a 2026-07-28 schema revision
entries.summary: The official Model Context Protocol (MCP) repository holds the spec, the protocol schema (TypeScript first, mirrored as JSON Schema) and the docs. Its README now points at a 2026-07-28 schema, replacing the 2025-11-25 version noted in an earlier entry. Spec changes go through working groups first, and only organization members may open pull requests.
entries.takeaway: Check MCP clients and servers against the 2026-07-28 schema; the README itself carries no new security content.

lessons.point: The canonical schema revision referenced by the repository is dated 2026-07-28.
lessons.excerpt: The schema is [defined in TypeScript](schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts) first

lessons.point: Spec changes need working-group approval before a pull request or SEP, so security proposals should go through a working group.
lessons.excerpt: are discussed and approved in the relevant working group

lessons.point: Outside contributors cannot open pull requests and must use issues or join a working group.
lessons.excerpt: may only be opened by members of the `modelcontextprotocol` GitHub organization.

actionable.title: Re-check MCP tooling against the 2026-07-28 schema
actionable.detail: Diff the 2026-07-28 schema against the version your MCP scanners, gateways and policy rules were built on, and update any field-level checks (for example tool metadata or authentication fields) that moved.

entries.title: Microsoft and NVIDIA say deployment context, not weight openness, sets open-weight risk
entries.summary: Microsoft and NVIDIA released a joint paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, built on ISO standards and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It sorts model risks into five categories (Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, Bias) and maps evaluations to selected risks. This first paper covers only the model layer, leaving runtime, harness and application layers to future work. The blog post also promotes Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls.
entries.takeaway: Teams that self-host open-weight models inherit safeguards a managed service would otherwise provide, so each risk needs an owner and a control at the layer where it can actually be enforced.

lessons.point: Risk comes from the model, use case, deployment and safeguards together. Whether the weights are open does not decide it.
lessons.excerpt: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.

lessons.point: A clean model evaluation says nothing about an agent's permissions, data access or tools. Those need their own assessment.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls.

lessons.point: Self-hosting moves responsibility for controls from the provider to the enterprise.
lessons.excerpt: enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service.

actionable.title: Map each self-hosted open-weight model risk to a control and an owner
actionable.detail: For each open-weight deployment, list the risks that apply under the five categories. Note which controls a managed service would have provided and which you now run yourself (filtering, access control, monitoring, human review). Attach an evaluation as evidence and name an accountable owner for each risk. Assess agent permissions, tools and runtime separately from the model evaluation. Revisit the mapping whenever the model or the deployment changes.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: supported; lesson 3 slightly firmer than the source's 'may take on' controls. Verifier novelty 15, relevance 40; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Nearest pool entry is the ProjectDiscovery LoRA-backdoored Qwen2.5-7B item ('Contain agents running third-party fine-tuned weights'), which shows a concrete open-weight attack. This item is a governance framework with no new attack or measurement. It aligns with the NIST AI RMF. What's new is a joint vendor taxonomy and an evaluation repository. The blog itself is mostly a promotion for the whitepaper.
entries.threat: Enterprises that self-host open-weight models may assume protections exist that a managed service would normally supply. They may also treat a model-level evaluation as proof that the agent or application built on it is safe.
entries.conditions: Applies when an enterprise runs its own open-weight model deployment, especially one connected to external data, tools or customer-facing workflows.
entries.mitigations: Map every identified risk to a control at the layer that can enforce it (model, inference environment, application or operations), and assess agent permissions, tools and runtime separately from the model.

entries.title: mcp-openapi-server exposes OpenAPI endpoints to agents as MCP tools
entries.summary: ivo-toby/mcp-openapi-server (301 stars) turns an OpenAPI specification into MCP tools over stdio or streamable HTTP, with static auth headers, mutual TLS and an AuthProvider for upstream calls. It can load all endpoints, only three dynamic meta-tools for discovery and invocation, or an explicit list, filtered by tag, resource path and HTTP method. The README warns that these filters shape the tool list and are not authorization, and it supports server instructions that a client may place in the model's system prompt.

lessons.point: Hiding endpoints from the tool list is not access control; the upstream API still has to enforce authorization.
lessons.excerpt: Tag filters are tool-surface controls, not authorization. Keep protecting sensitive endpoints with the upstream

lessons.point: A dynamic mode exposes only discovery and invoke meta-tools instead of one tool per endpoint, which keeps tool definitions small. In dynamic mode the README says only `--exclude-tag` applies, and does not say whether the other include filters do.
lessons.excerpt: Load only dynamic meta-tools (`list-api-endpoints`, `get-api-endpoint-schema`, `invoke-api-endpoint`)

lessons.point: Server instructions travel in the initialize result and can land in the system prompt, so whoever controls the server controls that text.
lessons.excerpt: the text travels in the `initialize` result, and a client may add it to the system prompt of the model

entries.takeaway: A useful OpenAPI-to-MCP bridge, but its filters narrow what the model sees, not what it can do; keep authorization in the API.

actionable.title: Scope the API credential, not just the tool list
actionable.detail: When bridging an OpenAPI spec to an agent, give the server a credential scoped to the endpoints you intend to expose, use explicit tool mode for sensitive APIs, and remember dynamic mode's invoke tool can call any endpoint not excluded by tag (untagged endpoints are not affected by exclude-tag).

entries.verify_note: Dynamic-mode lesson softened: README only says --exclude-tag applies there.
entries.prior_art: openapi-mcp-generator 5.0; Stainless's OpenAPI-to-MCP write-up.
entries.author: ivo-toby

entries.title: mcp-watch is an open-source static scanner for MCP server repositories
entries.summary: mcp-watch is a 139-star npm and Docker command-line tool that scans a GitHub URL or local MCP server project for hardcoded credentials, tool poisoning, prompt injection, tool mutation (rug-pull) risks, ANSI escape-sequence hiding, server spoofing, command injection, server-side request forgery and path traversal. It outputs console or JSON results with severity and category filters and exits non-zero on critical or high findings, which suits a continuous integration gate. The README lists its research sources but shows no detection rates, rule details or evaluation.

lessons.point: It tries to flag tool mutation, the risk that a server changes its tool definitions after approval, alongside static tool-description checks.
lessons.excerpt: Detects dynamic tool changes and rug-pull risks

lessons.point: The exit code is designed for gating builds on critical or high findings. Exit code 1 also signals a scan error, so a gate cannot tell a finding from a crash.
lessons.excerpt: No critical or high severity vulnerabilities found

lessons.point: The author positions it as one layer only; there is no published accuracy data to judge it by.
lessons.excerpt: This tool identifies potential security issues but should not be the only security measure.

entries.takeaway: Another unevaluated MCP repository scanner; trial it beside established scanners rather than relying on it.

actionable.title: Compare mcp-watch against an existing MCP scanner on known-bad servers
actionable.detail: Run mcp-watch scan-local --format json and an established scanner (for example Cisco's mcp-scanner) on a few deliberately poisoned MCP servers and a few clean ones; keep it in continuous integration only if it catches findings the other misses without excess false positives.

entries.verify_note: README-only scanner, no published evaluation.
entries.prior_art: Cisco AI Defense mcp-scanner; Invariant mcp-scan.
entries.author: kapilduraphe

entries.kind_reason: Vendor product launch and strategy post spanning many products, not a single patch notice.
entries.title: Microsoft launches Perception and agent-governance tools at Ignite, framing agents as insiders
entries.summary: This is Microsoft's Ignite 2026 marketing post. It announces Microsoft Perception, a set of red, blue and green team security agents, plus agent discovery and identity features in Agent 365 and Entra, and an AI Transparency Initiative. It also cites market figures, such as a PHP exploit built within about a day and only 26% of CISA known exploited vulnerabilities fixed in 2025. Most capabilities are in preview and nothing is independently evaluated.

lessons.point: Vendors frame AI agents as insiders with broad access that can err, be manipulated or be compromised, so they need identity and governance like staff.
lessons.excerpt: Agents are the new insiders.

lessons.point: Agent discovery and identity are the control plane Microsoft is pushing: local coding agents get a directory identity and Conditional Access.
lessons.excerpt: Discovery expands by 35 local agent types, to 60 in total, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot

lessons.point: Task-scoped, time-bound permissions for agents are an announced direction, but remain in limited preview.
lessons.excerpt: dynamic permissions grant task-scoped, time-bound access

lessons.point: Microsoft admits its containment tools do not reveal how an agent's model behaves, motivating a transparency initiative.
lessons.excerpt: they will not give them insight into how the model behind an agent behaves

entries.takeaway: Vendor roadmap, not evidence: it signals that agent identity, discovery and scoped access are becoming standard enterprise controls, but verify preview claims before relying on them.

actionable.title: Inventory agents and give each its own identity
actionable.detail: Whatever the vendor, discover local and cloud agents, assign each a distinct identity, scope its permissions to the task and time window, and log what it was asked to do. Treat Microsoft's preview features as roadmap until you can test them.

entries.prior_art: ai-security.json 'Microsoft frames agents as insiders and announces Dynamic Permissions and Guardian Agents' (Oct 19 2026) already covers agents-as-insiders, discovery of 60 local agent types incl. Claude Code/Codex, Entra Agent ID and task-scoped time-bound Dynamic Permissions; the Oct 2026 Agent 365 entries cover the rest.
entries.threat: Agents with broad access to data, apps and tools can be mistaken, manipulated or compromised, and AI speeds attackers' vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
entries.conditions: Claims come from vendor marketing. Many capabilities are preview-only or arrive in January 2027, and some require specific Microsoft licences.
entries.mitigations: Discover agents, give each an identity, apply Conditional Access and task-scoped time-bound permissions, contain local agents with device policy, and monitor runtime behaviour.

entries.title: United Airlines bans third-party AI agents from booking flights for travelers
entries.summary: United Airlines said it will restrict unauthorized third-party personal AI agents from making reservations (with check-in as the regulatory example), both on its own platforms and via travel agencies and aggregators. It cited the risk of sharing account credentials with such agents, unintended purchases, account changes or MileagePlus use, and possible violation of federal rules such as in-person hazardous-materials attestations at check-in. An analyst also attributes the move to keeping control of the customer relationship and avoiding the cost of AI bot flight searches.

lessons.point: United cites sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants as exposing sensitive information and risking unintended purchases, account changes or MileagePlus use.
lessons.excerpt: sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases

lessons.point: Some agent actions carry regulatory attestations a human must make in person, so delegating them may be non-compliant.
lessons.excerpt: could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances

lessons.point: Security framing can overlap with commercial motives: an analyst ties the ban to control of the booking channel and search cost.
lessons.excerpt: Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches.

entries.takeaway: United is blocking credential-sharing AI agents, which pushes agent builders toward scoped, sanctioned access instead of password reuse.

actionable.title: Do not build consumer agents on users' shared passwords
actionable.detail: For agents that transact on a user's behalf, use sanctioned integrations or scoped delegated tokens, keep a human confirmation step for purchases and loyalty-point spends, and do not automate steps that need a personal attestation (such as hazardous-materials check-in declarations).

entries.verify_note: The verifier found lesson 1 inferred (platform cannot tell agent from owner); it now states only the risks United cites, and the summary and takeaway were trimmed to the source.
entries.prior_art: 'Major US banks are blocking customers' third-party AI agents' already covers the same pattern (platforms blocking credential-sharing personal agents, with scoped delegated access as the fix); United extends it to airlines. Verifier's closest: 'Major US banks are blocking customers' third-party AI agents' entry.

entries.title: Tamga's prompt-injection rules caught 27 of 203 attacks written by others
entries.author: yatuk
entries.summary: Tamga is a self-hosted proxy for the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs that blocks or redacts PII, secrets and prompt injection under a YAML policy, with Turkish and English support. Its README reports that its injection rules score precision 1.000 and recall 0.910 on the author's own tuning corpus, but catch only 27 of 203 and 2 of 59 attacks in two Turkish sets written by others. The authors say the rules match wording, so attacks with no override phrase mostly get through.
entries.takeaway: Tamga's own numbers show a wording-based injection filter catching few attacks that someone else wrote, so test any such filter on independent attack sets.

lessons.point: Near-perfect scores on the author's own corpus did not transfer to attack sets written by others.
lessons.excerpt: | Turkish sets written by others, rules alone | 27 of 203 and 2 of 59 attacks caught, no benign prompt flagged |

lessons.point: The rules match phrasing, so attacks without an override phrase mostly get past them.
lessons.excerpt:
The rules match wording. Attacks with no override phrase (a persona, a task
slipped in after a question) mostly get past them;

lessons.point: The scan stage adds little latency, so cost is not the reason to skip a proxy filter.
lessons.excerpt: **Latency.** The scan stage takes p50 0.2 ms and p95 0.7 to 0.8 ms

actionable.title: Measure any injection filter on attacks its authors did not write
actionable.detail: Before buying or deploying a prompt-injection filter, run it on a held-out attack set from a different author (and in your users' languages); treat its result as a detection signal layered on containment, never as the boundary.

entries.verify_note: Lessons hold, but the verifier judged novelty 18 vs 45: the held-out collapse of phrase-matching injection filters is known (e.g. Hackett et al. 2025 on bypassing guardrail detectors); Tamga's two held-out sets are small and Turkish-only.
entries.prior_art: Self-reported results for LLM Guard, NeMo Guardrails and Lakera, and the pool's claim that input filtering cannot prevent prompt injection; Tamga's delta is publishing its own held-out collapse.
entries.threat: Prompt injection bypassing a rule-based input filter.
entries.conditions: Applications relying on a wording-based proxy filter for prompt-injection defence.
entries.mitigations: Layer filters with privilege separation and tool-call containment, and evaluate on independent attack sets.

entries.title: MCP ZAP Server blocks private-network targets and binds scan credentials server-side
entries.summary: mcp-zap-server lets AI agents drive the OWASP ZAP web scanner over MCP, behind API-key or JWT authentication, tool scopes, policy bundles and rate limits. The v0.17.1 README states the defaults: target URLs on localhost, private networks or link-local addresses are blocked, and published ports bind only to loopback. When target login is enabled, the server binds a stored credential to one approved origin, and callers pass only a profile ID and target URL. The pool already covers its distroless runtime, so the only new material here is the target and credential restrictions.

lessons.point: An MCP server that lets an agent send scanner traffic to URLs it chooses needs a default block on internal targets. Otherwise prompt-steered agents can probe the internal network.
lessons.excerpt: URL validation blocks localhost, private networks, and link-local targets by default.

lessons.point: Target credentials stay on the server and are tied to one approved origin. The agent never handles secrets and cannot point them at another site.
lessons.excerpt: guided auth binds an exact server-side credential reference and login settings to one approved origin; callers provide only `profileId` and `targetUrl`.

lessons.point: The runtime image is still digest-pinned and distroless with no shell. The pool already records this.
lessons.excerpt: The Java 25 JVM image uses a digest-pinned distroless runtime with no shell or

entries.takeaway: If you expose a scanner or other outbound tool to agents, block internal destinations by default and keep credentials server-side behind opaque profile IDs, so the agent chooses which approved profile to use but never what the secret is or where it goes.

actionable.title: Apply target denylists and opaque credential profiles to MCP tools that make outbound calls
actionable.detail: For any MCP tool that takes a URL, reject localhost, RFC1918 and link-local destinations unless an operator has explicitly allowlisted them. Store target credentials server-side, keyed by a profile ID that is bound to one origin, so the tool call carries only profileId and targetUrl.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all three lessons are verbatim README defaults; the repo is already in the pool, so novelty lowered to the verifier's 12.
entries.prior_art: The pool entry 'MCP ZAP Server Hardens Its Own Attack Surface by Shipping a Distroless Runtime With No Shell or curl' covers the same repo, including its distroless runtime and operator controls. The only new material is the private-network URL block and the origin-bound server-side credential profiles.
entries.threat: An agent driven by injected or untrusted context could point an MCP-exposed web scanner at internal hosts, or misuse target credentials against sites they were not meant for.
entries.conditions: The MCP ZAP server is deployed with agents allowed to choose scan targets, especially in shared or networked deployments where ports are not bound only to loopback.
entries.mitigations: Keep the defaults: API-key or JWT auth, loopback-bound ports and the block on localhost, private and link-local targets. Bind target credentials server-side to single approved origins. Use tool scopes, rate limits and audit events, and review the production checklist before widening access.
